name: AP Seminar
overview: AP Seminar is the first course in the AP Capstone program. Students investigate real-world issues from multiple perspectives, analyze arguments and evidence, synthesize sources into their own arguments, and communicate through essays and presentations. Skills are organized by the QUEST framework: Question and Explore, Understand and Analyze, Evaluate Multiple Perspectives, Synthesize Ideas, and Team, Transform, and Transmit.
examMode: End-of-course exam is fully digital in Bluebook; performance tasks are submitted through the AP Digital Portfolio

sections.name: Performance Task 1
sections.notes: Completed during the year with a team: research on a problem, then a team multimedia presentation with individual oral defense questions.

sections.name: Performance Task 2
sections.notes: Completed during the year from College Board stimulus materials: an individual written argument, a multimedia presentation, and an oral defense.

sections.name: End-of-course exam, Part A
sections.notes: Read one argument and answer three questions: identify the author's argument or main idea, explain the line of reasoning, and evaluate the evidence. Part A is about 30% of the exam score.

sections.name: End-of-course exam, Part B
sections.notes: Read four sources on a theme, identify a research question or issue, and write an evidence-based argument using at least two of the sources. Part B is about 70% of the exam score.

skills.name: Question and Explore
skills.description: Ask focused questions, choose lenses, and find and evaluate sources.

skills.name: Understand and Analyze
skills.description: Identify an argument's claims, line of reasoning, and evidence, and judge how well they work.

skills.name: Evaluate Multiple Perspectives
skills.description: Compare perspectives, find where they agree and differ, and judge their strengths and limits.

skills.name: Synthesize Ideas
skills.description: Combine evidence into your own argument, address other views, and cite sources properly.

skills.name: Team, Transform, and Transmit
skills.description: Collaborate, adapt communication to an audience, and reflect on the process.

scoring.summary: Team project and presentation 20%, individual essay and presentation 35%, end-of-course exam 45%. On the exam, Part A (three short answers) is about 30% and Part B (the argument essay) about 70%. Responses are scored with analytic rubric rows. Klutch's practice tasks use simplified point scales, not the official ones.

frqTypes.name: Part A Q1: Identify the argument
frqTypes.howScored: Klutch practice scale: the main claim, the key supporting reasons, and an accurate paraphrase that doesn't distort the author's position.

frqTypes.name: Part A Q2: Explain the line of reasoning
frqTypes.howScored: Klutch practice scale: identifies the claims, explains how they connect logically toward the conclusion, and does so accurately and in order.

frqTypes.name: Part A Q3: Evaluate the evidence
frqTypes.howScored: Klutch practice scale: names specific evidence, judges its relevance and credibility, and explains how its strengths and limits affect the argument.

frqTypes.name: Part B: Argument essay
frqTypes.howScored: Klutch practice scale: a clear argument (3), evidence from at least two sources (3), engagement with other perspectives (2), a logical line of reasoning (2), and clear writing with attribution (2).

frqTypes.name: Skill task
frqTypes.howScored: Unit-specific practice tasks (research questions, source evaluation, oral defense) scored by the rubric shown with each task.

strategy: In Part A, spend the first minutes mapping the passage: the main claim, each reason, and the evidence for each.
Answer Part A Q1 in two or three sentences; it rewards accuracy, not length.
For Part A Q3, judge evidence by relevance, credibility, and sufficiency, and say how each strength or weakness affects the argument.
In Part B, write a research question you can actually argue about, then build the argument from at least two sources (three is safer), using their ideas, not just quotes.
Address an opposing or alternative perspective and respond to it; this is what separates high Part B scores.
Attribute every source in the text ('According to the economist in Source C...').
pitfalls: Summarizing sources in Part B instead of making your own argument.
Calling evidence 'credible' without explaining why (author expertise, publication, method, date).
Picking a Part B question so broad that the essay becomes a list of facts.
Agreeing with every source; synthesis means showing how ideas relate, including tensions.
In presentations, reading slides aloud instead of speaking to the audience.
caveats: Performance-task components and rubrics are revised periodically; check AP Central for the current task directions.
Point values on Klutch's practice tasks are simplified practice scales, not College Board's rubric rows.
All practice passages and sources are written by Klutch; authors and data in them are fictional unless stated otherwise.
